title: LLMs can understand and write neural network weights
content:
The complete logs of every experiment in the blog post Sparks of Weight Space Programming: LLMs can understand and write neural network weights. For each experiment you get:
- everything we sent the model;
- everything it sent back, including its reasoning summaries;
- every piece of code it ran, with the output it saw;
- the evaluation behind each number in the post;
- the networks it read or wrote.
Each experiment folder has its own README. It says which run is which tab or row in the post, and which file each number comes from.
Only the runs the post reports are here. Trial runs of earlier prompt versions are left out.
"Astra" in the post is OpenAI's gpt-6-astra.
One turn. Every turn is one call of the Codex CLI: codex exec, or codex exec resume <thread> to continue a
conversation. The prompt goes in on stdin. The reasoning effort is set per call and recorded in each turn's run.json:
No tools of its own. Every built-in Codex capability that gives the model a tool is switched off: shell, file
editing, web search, image viewing, sub-agents, plugins and the rest. The configuration is in
harness/codex_config.toml, and the system instructions are one neutral line,
harness/instructions.md. Each call names the model and the effort itself, overriding
the defaults in that file.
Every turn was audited. We checked each turn's event stream. A turn counts as tool-free when the stream holds only
the model's messages, its reasoning summaries, and Codex's notice that code mode is disabled. The result is the
audit.tool_free field of the turn's run.json. All 1,125 turns in this release are tool-free.
Where code was allowed (Experiments 3, 6, 7, 8):
- The model wrote one Python block per turn.
- We ran it in our own sandbox (harness/sandbox.py): bubblewrap, no network, a working folder
kept between runs, and a time limit per run.
- We sent the printed output back as the next message.
- Each run's code and output are in tool_calls.jsonl.
- What the code was allowed to do is stated in the experiment's prompt and in its README.
Not every file appears in every run.
Placeholders. Internal paths are replaced by placeholders:
Codex thread ids are replaced by id- and 8 hex digits. The same thread keeps the same id in every file, so turns
of one conversation still match up.
- The Gemma 3 270M fine-tunes of Experiment 7 (17 GB). The data, the training script and the hashes are there, so they can be rebuilt.
- The intermediate files the model wrote while working: activations, generated-text dumps and its draft networks. The final networks and weight edits are included, Experiment 8's as exact diffs against the public base weights, with a script that applies them.
- The text of Experiment 3's Python corpus. It is other projects' code, so we give a manifest and a rebuild script instead.
- The GPQA question texts in Experiment 8's generations. GPQA's scores and per-question results are kept.
See LICENSE.
Third-party benchmark data keep their own licenses: MATH, GSM8K, IFEval, MMLU-Pro and the others in Experiment 8.

report.summary: A new log release documents experiments in which OpenAI's gpt-6-astra read and wrote neural network weights directly, across 1,125 audited tool-free turns.
report.background: Most work on what large models 'know' looks at activations — probing classifiers, prompting, chain-of-thought inspection. The weight space is rarer territory: parameters are high-dimensional, permutation-symmetric and awkward to tokenise, so treating them as something a model can read and write is counterintuitive. Interest has grown anyway, driven by hypernetworks, model merging, weight arithmetic and fact-editing research, all of which assume parameters carry structured, legible information. The blog post 'Sparks of Weight Space Programming' tests whether a frontier model can reason about another network's parameters directly. This repository is its evidence trail — not selected highlights but every prompt, reasoning summary, code block, sandbox output and evaluation script behind each reported number, published to address reproducibility concerns in LLM research.
key_points: The repository publishes the complete experimental record: every message sent to the model, every response including reasoning summaries, all executed code with its output, the evaluation behind each number in the post, and the networks the model read or wrote. Each experiment folder has a README mapping runs to specific tables and rows.

The protocol was deliberately austere. Every built-in Codex capability that could act as a tool — shell, file editing, web search, image viewing, sub-agents, plugins — was switched off, leaving a neutral one-line system instruction. An audit of each turn's event stream confirms all 1,125 turns were tool-free.

Code execution was permitted only in four experiments. The model wrote one Python block per turn, which ran in a bubblewrap sandbox with no network and a per-run time limit; printed output was returned as the next message, with code and output logged in tool_calls.jsonl.

Substantial artefacts are included or rebuildable: the Gemma 3 270M fine-tunes (17 GB) ship as data, training script and hashes, and Experiment 8's weight edits are stored as exact diffs against public base weights with an application script.

Some material is withheld for licensing: Experiment 3's Python corpus text is replaced by a manifest and rebuild script, and GPQA question texts are omitted while scores and per-question results are kept. Benchmark data retains its own licences.

Notably, 'Astra' in the post is identified as OpenAI's gpt-6-astra, and the harness records per-call model and reasoning-effort settings in each turn's run.json, making the exact configuration reproducible.
report.impact: If the claims hold up, this reframes what frontier models are for. Reading and writing weights would let models inspect, patch or compress other networks without retraining — useful for debugging, merging, pruning and targeted repair of deployed systems. For developers it suggests a workflow where an LLM edits parameters as a code artefact, with diffs and review, rather than only generating training scripts. For researchers, the release's value may be as much methodological as technical: turn-level audits, sandbox logs and per-number provenance set a bar that most capability papers do not meet. Ordinary users would see the effects indirectly, through cheaper adaptation of small models and more transparent claims about what AI systems can do. The main caveat is that results come from one model family and a small set of networks.
report.tools: Start with the repository itself (RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs), whose per-experiment READMEs map runs to results. Reproduce the harness with OpenAI's Codex CLI and bubblewrap for sandboxing, and Gemma 3 270M for the fine-tuning experiments. For weight inspection, pair it with TransformerLens or nnsight; for weight-diff workflows, the repo's apply script is a template. Watch the underlying blog post for interpretation and benchmark coverage (MATH, GSM8K, IFEval, MMLU-Pro, GPQA).
